title: The Tables of the Planets: Agrippa's Magic Squares, Seals and Characters (De occulta philosophia II.22)
otherNames: 'the sacred tables of the planets' (J.F. 1651, II.xxii, p. 239; verified in EEBO-TCP A26565)

kameas (modern Western occult usage, said to come from Hebrew qamea', 'amulet'. The word does not occur anywhere in the 1651 English: the whole EEBO-TCP A26565 text was searched, 0 hits. The 1533 Latin was not checked)
awfāq (Arabic, singular wafq: the Islamic magic-square tradition)
family: Numerical tables with seals and characters. This is not an alphabet; it is built on the values of the Hebrew letters.
summary: In Book II, chapter 22 of De occulta philosophia (first printed 1533; July 1533 by the colophon, as the McGill Library record is reported to say), Agrippa prints seven magic squares, one for each planet. They run from Saturn's 3×3, whose lines each add to 15, to the Moon's 9×9, whose lines add to 369. For each square he lists Hebrew divine names and an 'intelligence' and a 'spirit' (in the 1651 English; the Latin word, daemonium as recalled, was not checked) whose letters add up to the square's key numbers (Agiel and Zazel, both 45, for Saturn). He then prints the seal of the planet and the characters of its intelligence and spirit, and reports what 'they say' the table does when engraved on the planet's metal under a fortunate or an unfortunate planet. He does not explain how the seals are drawn; he leaves that to 'the wise searcher'. The squares are older than Agrippa: historians of mathematics report an Arabic art of magic squares by the 10th century and planetary squares in Latin manuscripts before 1533 (recalled scholarship, not re-checked here). No source earlier than Agrippa is named here for the names and seals.

firstAttestation.locator: Book II, chapter 22. In the 1651 English (EEBO-TCP A26565) the heading on p. 239 reads 'CHAP. XXII. Of the tables of the Planets, their vertues, forms, and what Divine names, Intelligencies, and Spirits are set over them.' The table of contents spells it 'Intelligences' and gives 'pag. 239'. The text runs pp. 239-242, the name lists are on p. 243, and the squares, their Hebrew versions ('In Hebrew notes') and the seals are on pp. 244-252: Saturn and Jupiter p. 244, Mars p. 245, Sun p. 246, Venus pp. 247-248, Mercury pp. 249-250, Moon pp. 251-252. Chapter 23 begins on p. 253. The 1533 page or signature is not verified.
firstAttestation.notes: This is the earliest attestation found here for this set of names, numbers and seals. It is not the first attestation of the squares. Trithemius's reply to Agrippa's manuscript draft, printed in the 1651 front matter, is dated 'From our Monastery of Peapolis, the 8. day of April, An. M. D. X.' (EEBO-TCP A26565), so the draft existed by 8 April 1510. The SEP entry is reported to place Agrippa's visit to Trithemius in the winter of 1509-10 and the draft's arrival shortly before 8 April 1510 (search-backed theban fact-check, theban.verified.json; not re-seen here). The draft is reported as Würzburg, Universitätsbibliothek, M. ch. q. 50 (sibling research; the checker's own recollection agrees; not seen). In 'To the Reader' Agrippa says that for the print 'we added some Chapters, and we inserted many things' (J.F. 1651, verified in EEBO-TCP), so II.22 cannot be dated to the draft without the manuscript. Perrone Compagni's critical edition (Brill, 1992) records the draft's readings and would settle it. Do not date the squares 'Agrippa 1510' or '1531'. Book II was first printed in 1533.

claims.claim: Agrippa assigns seven magic squares to the planets in the Chaldean order: Saturn 3×3, Jupiter 4×4, Mars 5×5, Sun 6×6, Venus 7×7, Mercury 8×8, Moon 9×9.
claims.evidence: Verified in J.F. 1651, II.xxii, pp. 239-242 (EEBO-TCP A26565): 'The first of them is assigned to Saturn, and consists of a square of three' ... 'The seventh table is of the Moon, of a square of nine'. The order is the descending (Chaldean) planetary order. The 1533 Latin was not seen. The 1651 English, as keyed, has a slip for Mars: 'made of a square of four containing twenty five numbers' (p. 240).

Recomputed in the fact-check for all seven squares as given: each holds 1 to n² once, and every row, column and main diagonal gives n(n²+1)/2. Agrippa states every line sum and total; verified in J.F. 1651: Saturn 'fifteen' and 'fourty five' (p. 239); Jupiter 'thirty four' and '136', Mars 'sixty five' and '325', Sun 111 (keyed 'III.') and '666' (p. 240); Venus '175' and '1225', Mercury '260' and '2080' (p. 241); Moon '369' and '3321' (p. 242).
sources: computation in this session and in the fact-check

claims.claim: Agrippa sets nearly every divine name, intelligence and spirit against one of the square's four key numbers (the side n, the number of cells n², the line sum or the total), and the letters of most add up to the number given.
claims.evidence: Computed from the Hebrew spellings in this file (the Hebrew is NOT checked: EEBO-TCP does not key Hebrew) against the numbers in J.F.'s name lists (1651, p. 243; many first digits are keyed as illegible). For Saturn: Ab 3 (side), Hod 9 (cells), Iah and Hod 15 (line sum), and 'Jehovah extended', Agiel and Zazel 45 (total). REFUTED in two places. (1) Mars is not an exception: the 1651 list has a fifth Mars entry numbered 25 (n²), printed in Hebrew only. (2) Venus is the exception: its fourth entry, Bne Seraphim, is numbered '[illegible]252' in 1651, not the total 1225. So the 1651 lists have 37 entries, not 36, and every square has a name at each of its four key numbers except Venus at its total. Where the intelligence and spirit sit varies: Saturn, Jupiter and Mars put both at the total; Sun and Mercury put the intelligence at the line sum and the spirit at the total; Venus puts Hagiel at n² (49), Kedemel at the line sum (175) and the plural Bne Seraphim at [1]252; the Moon puts Hasmodai, 'the spirit of the Moon', at the line sum and its two compound beings at the total. Of the 36 entries whose Hebrew this file gives, 32 add up with ordinary letter values; three (Bne Seraphim at its printed number and the Moon's two long names) only with the great final-letter values; Asboga only by its letter-pairs. Agrippa does not state the pattern; the observation is the researcher's.
sources: computation in this session and in the fact-check

claims.claim: Bne Seraphim's number, printed as [1]252 in 1651, is not the Venus square's total (1225).
claims.evidence: REFUTES the research file, which said Agrippa gives it as 1225 and that the name fits under neither convention. EEBO-TCP keys the 1651 entry as '[illegible digit]252 | Bne Seraphim | The Intelligencies of Venus' (p. 243). Computed: בני שרפים gives 692 with ordinary values and exactly 1252 if final mem counts 600. So the name fits its printed number with the great final value, but that number is not one of the square's key numbers. Whether 1252 is an error for 1225 or deliberate is not settled here. The keyed numbers in this list are unreliable (Kedemel, whose name and line sum are 175, is keyed '[?]67'), so check the 1651 page image and the 1533 plate before the page states the number. That Tyson (1993) discusses the problem is the researcher's recollection; not checked.

claims.claim: The Moon's two long names reach 3321 only if final letters take their 'great' values. Elim (81) and Din (64) need the ordinary values.
claims.evidence: Computed. Schedbarschemoth Schartathan (שדברשהמעת שרתתן) gives 2671 with ordinary values and 3321 if final nun is 700. For the second name the file's spelling מלכא בתרשיתים עד ברוח שחקים gives 2201, or 3321 with final mem as 600. J.F. 1651 (p. 243, EEBO-TCP) transliterates it 'Malcha betharsisim hed ber[illegible]ah schehalim', which points to shin (not tav) in the second word and lamed (not qoph) in the last. Computed: with shin and qoph 3221; with tav and lamed 3251; with shin and lamed 3151 (all with great finals). Only the file's tav-and-qoph spelling reaches 3321, so that spelling may be a reconstruction made to fit the number; it is not confirmed by the 1651 transliteration. The 1533 Hebrew was not seen. The lists are in any case not consistent about final letters (Elim 81 and Din 64 need the ordinary values). The 1651 headings call this being 'The Intelligency of the Intelligence of the Moon' (name list, p. 243) and 'the Intelligence of the Intelligences of the Moon' (seal caption, p. 252).
sources: computation in this session and in the fact-check

claims.claim: Asboga, set against 8 for Mercury and glossed 'eight extended', adds up to 24.
claims.evidence: Computed: א1+ז7+ב2+ו6+ג3+ה5 = 24. The six letters form three pairs that each make 8 (1+7, 2+6, 3+5), which probably explains 'eight extended'; that reading is the researcher's inference. The 1651 list reads 'A[illegible]boga, eight extended.' (p. 243, EEBO-TCP), number illegible. That Azbogah also occurs in Hekhalot literature (3 Enoch) is recalled by researcher and checker; not checked.

claims.claim: The intelligence presides over the good effects of the table and the spirit (daemonium) over the evil ones.
claims.evidence: Agrippa's own distinction. J.F. 1651, p. 239 (EEBO-TCP A26565), on Saturn: names that 'fill up the numbers with an Intelligency to what is good, with a spirit to what is bad'. The formula recurs for every planet (e.g. Jupiter, p. 240: 'with an Intelligence to good, with a spirit to bad'). It is his doctrine, reported as such. That the Latin word J.F. renders 'spirit' is daemonium is recalled, not checked against the 1533 text.

claims.claim: The seals of the planets and the characters of the intelligences and spirits are drawn out of the numbers of the squares.
claims.evidence: Agrippa says so: J.F. 1651, p. 239 (EEBO-TCP A26565), 'out of the same numbers is drawn the seal, or Character of Saturn, and of the spirits thereof'. At the end of the chapter (p. 242) he declines to give the method: 'Now how the seals, and Characters of the Stars, and spirits are drawn from these tables, the wise searcher, and he which shall understand the verifying of these tables, shall easily find out.' The statement is documented; the method is not.

claims.claim: A name's character is made by reducing each letter to a number that is on the square and joining the cells in order.
claims.evidence: This explanation is attributed to Golden Dawn teaching and modern commentators (Tyson 1993); both are recalled, not checked. Agrippa does not state it; he leaves the method to 'the wise searcher' (J.F. 1651, p. 242). It cannot be the whole story. Recomputed in the fact-check: on Saturn's 3×3, Agiel (1, 3, 10→1, 1, 30→3) visits only two cells, so its path is a single line run back and forth. If the printed character of Agiel is more than that (not seen), the simple method does not produce it. Present the method as a modern reconstruction.

claims.claim: Each planet's seal is a figure that passes through every cell of its square.
claims.evidence: LOW CONFIDENCE. This is a claim I associate with modern commentary on the seals. It could not be checked, because the plates were not seen in this session. Do not state it on the page without checking it against the 1533 plate.

claims.claim: The squares come from the Arabic (Islamic) magic-square tradition.
claims.evidence: This is a scholarly judgement about a general lineage, not a documented line of copying, so it is now 'attributed'. As the researcher recalls them, historians of mathematics document a developed Arabic art of magic squares from the 10th century (Sesiano 2017, 2019; Cammann 1969) and report Latin texts on the seven planetary squares, adapted from Arabic, before 1533 (Folkerts 1981). None of these works was checked here. Agrippa's odd squares follow the construction rule stated in the units (recomputed); that the rule belongs to that tradition rests on recall of Sesiano. The manuscript Agrippa used is not identified. The page should say whose judgement this is.

claims.claim: Agrippa took the planetary squares from Picatrix.
claims.evidence: I know of no set of planetary magic squares in the Latin Picatrix (ed. Pingree, 1986); not checked in this session. Picatrix shares the wider frame: images engraved on the planet's metal at an astrologically chosen hour, with good or ill effects according to the planet's condition. Do not name it as the source of the squares unless the passage is found. The checker likewise knows of no magic squares in Picatrix (own knowledge; not checked).

claims.claim: Agrippa took the squares from Cardano.
claims.evidence: The dates rule it out. Cardano's Practica arithmetice was printed at Milan in 1539 (recalled), six years after Agrippa's July 1533 print (colophon date per the McGill record, reported by the theban fact-check). If there is a debt, it more likely runs from Agrippa to Cardano, or both drew on a common source.

claims.claim: The Saturn square's use to help childbirth continues the Islamic use of the 3×3 square (budūḥ) to ease labour.
claims.evidence: The parallel is recalled, not checked: the 3×3 square, called budūḥ after the letters of its corner values (2, 4, 6, 8), was used in Islamic practice to ease childbirth and is associated with al-Ghazālī (Cammann; Sesiano). The researcher says the ascription comes from later sources; the checker recalls that al-Ghazālī himself, in al-Munqidh min al-ḍalāl, mentions a 3×3 square drawn on two cloths for a woman in labour. Neither version is verified, so the page should not say which. Agrippa's first virtue of the Saturn table is verified: J.F. 1651, pp. 239-240, 'doth help to bring forth, or birth'. A line of descent is not documented. Offer this as a parallel.

claims.claim: The 3×3 square was revealed to the emperor Yu on the back of a turtle from the river Luo (the Luoshu).
claims.evidence: Chinese legend, reported as legend. Versions differ on the details (the checker knows it as a turtle from the Luo river in the time of Yu the Great). That the arrangement itself is attested in Chinese texts of the Han period is recalled (Cammann); the date and text are not verified. No link to Agrippa is documented.

claims.claim: Sorath, the spirit of the Sun, equals 666, the number of the beast in Revelation 13:18.
claims.evidence: The arithmetic is exact: ס60+ו6+ר200+ת400 = 666, the total of the 6×6 square. In II.xxii the 1651 English says only 'the sum of all is 666' (p. 240) and lists 'Sorath | The spirit of the Sun' (p. 243); the chapter has no reference to Revelation or the beast (EEBO-TCP searched). But Agrippa does cite Revelation 13:18 elsewhere in Book II, as an example of the power of name-numbers: II.iii (p. 173) and II.xx (p. 237), 'Let him which hath understanding compute the number of the name of the beast, which is the number of a man'. He never ties it to Sorath or the Sun's square. Report the arithmetic, and say that any link to Sorath is modern inference.
sources: J.F. 1651, II.iii p. 173, II.xx p. 237, II.xxii pp. 240 and 243 (EEBO-TCP A26565)

claims.claim: Agrippa calls the squares 'kameas'.
claims.evidence: Not in the English: the word does not occur anywhere in the 1651 translation (whole EEBO-TCP A26565 text searched, 0 hits). J.F. writes 'tables' ('the sacred tables of the planets', p. 239; 'The Table of Saturn in his compass', p. 244). The Latin word (tabulae, as the researcher recalls) was not checked. That 'kamea' for a planetary square belongs to 19th-century and later Western occultism is recalled, not checked.

claims.claim: Agrippa's 1510 draft already contained the planetary squares.
claims.evidence: Unknown here. The draft (reported as Würzburg UB M. ch. q. 50) existed by 8 April 1510, the date of Trithemius's reply (1651 front matter, verified). Agrippa says that for the print 'we added some Chapters' ('To the Reader', 1651, verified). Perrone Compagni's 1992 edition would show whether II.22 was in the draft. Agrippa's years in Italy (c. 1511-1518; recalled) and Pacioli's manuscript (recalled) would make the later revision a plausible time for the addition, but this is conjecture.

claims.claim: The names Agiel, Zazel, Iophiel, Hismael and the rest were known before Agrippa.
claims.evidence: No earlier witness was found or checked. Several divine names are biblical (Ab, Iah, Adonai, Eloh, Elim, El Ab). Azbogah has, as recalled, a Hekhalot pedigree. Agrippa himself, in Book III, presents Zazel as a demon of Hebrew tradition: J.F. 1651, III.xviii, p. 401 ('which they understand of Zazell, and his Army', citing 'the Cabalists') and III.xli, p. 475 ('as say the divines of the Hebrews, is left in the power of the Demon Zazel'). letters.name: Table (square) of Saturn
letters.form: A grid of 3×3 square cells with one number in each cell. Read row by row from the top, left to right: 4 9 2 / 3 5 7 / 8 1 6. Every row, column and main diagonal adds to 15; all the numbers together add to 45. Computed here. This square is exactly what you get by the following rule. Put 1 in the cell directly below the centre. Step one cell down and one to the right, wrapping round the edges. When that cell is already taken, go two cells straight down from the last number instead. The centre always holds the middle number, (n²+1)/2. The rule identifies the arrangement; it is not a claim about how Agrippa or his source built it.
letters.note: Fact-check: matches the 1651 table ('The Table of Saturn in his compass', p. 244, EEBO-TCP A26565) cell for cell, in the same orientation. The 1651 English prints each table again 'In Hebrew notes' (as figures not keyed by TCP); whether 1533 does is not verified. Before drawing, check cell by cell against the 1533 plate, which was not seen.
